title: Orodental pathology in Mosasaurus hoffmannii (Reptilia: Squamata)
content:
Abstract
Mosasaurus hoffmannii is a gigantic and well-studied taxon of mosasaur, first excavated from the Maastricht Formation in the Netherlands over 250 years ago. Here, we use μCT imaging to examine two M. hoffmannii skulls from the Maastricht Formation of Belgium, which have severe pathologies that were originally identified as infected fractures. The first of these pathologies, in a subadult skull, is actually a misaligned alveolus. Trauma to the dentary probably inverted the developing tooth and atrophied the dental lamina, causing massive inflammation and resorption as the tooth grew towards the tongue. The second, in a large adult, is indeed a non-union fracture, but signs of ‘infection’ are alternatively interpreted here as resorption due to persistent inflammation at the site of an unstable fracture; this specimen exhibited a pseudoarthrosis, probably perpetuated by the inability of the kinetic mandible to heal straight. This specimen also shows probable bite marks, including one that severed the alveolar canal, though signs of neurovascular reattachment are present here. These specimens add to the growing record documenting the violent lives of giant mosasaurids, and further highlight the challenges their kinetic anatomies posed to normal vertebrate healing processes.
